judgments.title: NG YIN PIN v DEREK KWOK KEE YEUNG & ors
judgments.catchwords: 1 . This is a divorce proceeding commenced by Ng Yin Ping ("the Petitioner Wife") against Derek Kwok Kee Yeung ("the Respondent Husband"). In the Petition, the Petitioner Wife seeks, inter alia, various reliefs arising from the breakdown of the marriage. The Petitioner Wife has also named Olga, Marianne Rostaqui ep. Petithomme ("the Co-Respondent") as the Co-Respondent in respect of allegations concerning the Respondent Husband's alleged adultery with the Co-Respondent. 2. The Respondent Husband filed his Answer to the Petition and Cross-Petition dated 26 November 2025. In his Cross-Petition, the Respondent Husband named Kang Cheow Sean ("the Party Cited") in respect of allegations that the Party Cited was involved in an adulterous relationship with the Petitioner Wife. The Respondent Husband further seeks, inter alia, an order that the Party Cited pay damages to him for adultery. 3. The present judgment concerns the Party Cited's application in Enclosure 19 to be struck out and/or removed as a party to the Respondent Husband's Answer and Cross-Petition. The application is made pursuant to Order 18 rule 19 and Order 92 rule 4 of the Rules of Court 2012, read with rule 103 of the Divorce and Matrimonial Proceedings Rules 1980. 4. The issue for determination is whether, in the circumstances of the present case, the Party Cited ought to be struck out and/or removed as a party to the Respondent Husband's Answer and Cross-Petition on the grounds that the pleadings disclose no reasonable cause of action against him and/or that his inclusion is scandalous, frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of the process of the Court.

control sufficient to satisfy “likely to have or have had” requirement — Resignation not conclusive of loss of all access or copies — No evidence of present possession — Utility of production judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya v CHAN WEN JIE
judgments.catchwords: Child Act 2001 – Section 31(1)(a) – Ill-treatment of child – Guilty plea – Caregiver entrusted with custody of 3-year-old child – CCTV footage showing repeated abuse including caning, slapping, striking victim's head, forcing squat-thrusts, prolonged standing and consumption of excrement – Victim sustained 44 superficial injuries – Whether sentence should reflect cruelty and humiliation inflicted upon victim. Criminal Sentencing – Principles – Balance between public interest and offender's interest – Court required to consider seriousness of offence, aggravating and mitigating factors and sentencing trends – Sentence must be proportionate to offence actually convicted. Mitigation – Guilty plea – First offender – Remorse – Cooperation with authorities – Prompt medical assistance rendered to victim – Discount available for early plea though capable of reduction where offence involved significant cruelty. Aggravating Factors – Breach of trust – Accused paid to care for victim – Victim aged three years and unable to defend himself – Repeated abuse resulting in 44 injuries – Humiliating and degrading treatment – Forced consumption of excrement constituting exceptionally cruel conduct. Sentencing – Withdrawn charge – Murder charge under s 302 Penal Code subsequently withdrawn – Withdrawn charge cannot be treated as aggravating factor – Accused to be regarded as innocent of withdrawn charge. Sentencing – Relevant facts – Victim's death – Medical evidence showing death not subject matter of conviction – Death cannot be considered as aggravating factor where accused convicted only of child abuse under s 31(1)(a) Child Act 2001. Sentencing Trend – Section 31 Child Act 2001 – Cases involving death or grievous injuries generally attracting imprisonment of 10 years or more – Cases involving superficial injuries attracting sentences ranging from 15 months to 5 years – Present case justified higher sentence due to extreme humiliation and cruelty. Evidence – CCTV recording – Objective visual evidence of repeated abuse – Court entitled to place substantial weight on CCTV footage demonstrating nature, frequency and degree of mistreatment inflicted on child victim. Child Abuse – Humiliation as aggravating feature – Forcing victim to eat excrement from diaper found to be an extreme form of mistreatment and degradation – Serious aggravating factor warranting enhancement of custodial sentence beyond ordinary abuse cases involving superficial injuries. Sentence – 8 years and 6 months' imprisonment from date of arrest – Bond of good behaviour with one surety for three years – Community service of 36 hours within six months pursuant to s 31(2) Child Act 2001. Ratio Decidendi: In sentencing under s 31(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001, the court must impose a punishment proportionate to the offence of conviction and cannot take into account a withdrawn murder charge or the victim's death if they do not form part of the conviction. However, exceptional cruelty, humiliation, breach of trust and sustained abuse of a vulnerable child may justify a substantial custodial sentence notwithstanding the presence of mitigating factors and an early guilty plea. Keywords: Child abuse; ill-treatment of child; caregiver; breach of trust; guilty plea; sentencing principles; aggravating factors; mitigating factors; CCTV evidence; humiliation; forced consumption of excrement; proportionality; withdrawn charge; victim's death; Child Act 2001; community service.
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Abdul Fareed bin Abdul Gafoor

judgments.title: XXXX & ors v Dr Sumayyah binti Mohd Faridz & ors

parties.label: DEFENDAN
names: Dr Nur Zawani binti Mohd Zain

judgments.catchwords: 1. This action arises from injuries sustained by the 1st Plaintiff during her birth at Hospital Melaka on 18 February 2018. The claim is founded upon allegations of medical negligence in the management of labour and delivery which resulted in severe and permanent neurological injury to the 1st Plaintiff. 2. Following the close of the Plaintiffs’ case, the 11th Defendant (D11) admitted liability. Accordingly, the sole issue remaining for determination is the assessment of damages consequent upon the injuries sustained by the 1st Plaintiff. 3. The evidence establishes that the 1st Plaintiff suffers from spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy, severe developmental impairment, recurrent seizure disorder, scoliosis and lifelong dependency upon others for the ordinary activities of daily living. 4. The assessment of damages in a case of this nature is an exercise of considerable difficulty. No award of damages is capable of restoring the life which the 1st Plaintiff would otherwise have enjoyed. 5. The law nevertheless requires the Court to award fair and reasonable compensation for the injuries sustained and the consequences flowing therefrom. 6. These grounds set out the Court's reasons for the assessment of damages, including the treatment of expert evidence, compliance with case management directions, future care requirements, multiplier determination and aggravated damages.
